rows.label: Balanced Ryser counterexamples at prime orders

value.scope:
Ryser's covering conjecture predicts that an intersecting $r$-partite hypergraph has a vertex cover of size at most $r-1$. The formalization proves that every sufficiently large prime $q$ has a finite intersecting $(q+1)$-partite, $(q+1)$-uniform hypergraph with covering number $q+1$ and exactly $q+1$ nonisolated vertices in each part. Thus the conjecture fails even with equal part sizes. The prime threshold is existential.

Ryser's covering conjecture predicts $	au\le(r-1)
u$ for an $r$-partite hypergraph, where $	au$ and $
u$ are its covering and matching numbers. The formalized constructions give finite intersecting $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraphs with $
u=1$ and $	au=r$, contradicting the bound. The ranks have the form $r=p^n+1$: one fixed prime $p\equiv2\pmod3$ works for all sufficiently large prime degrees $n$, and a second result covers every sufficiently large such prime $p$ and every sufficiently large odd $n$, with the degree threshold allowed to depend on $p$. Infinitely many ranks occur. Equal part sizes and numerical thresholds are not asserted.

statements.name: thm:main
statements.text:
\label{thm:main}
There exists $s_0$ such that, for every prime $s\ge s_0$ with
$s\equiv2\pmod3$, there is an integer $n_0(s)\ge3$ with the following
property. For every odd integer $n\ge n_0(s)$, put $q=s^n$.
There is a finite intersecting $(q+1)$-partite $(q+1)$-uniform
hypergraph $H$ satisfying
\[
 \tau(H)=q+1.
\]
In particular, the intersecting case of~\eqref{eq:ryser} is false.

statements.name: thm:main
statements.text:
\label{thm:main}
There exists $q_0$ such that, for every prime $q\ge q_0$, there is a
finite intersecting $(q+1)$-partite $(q+1)$-uniform hypergraph $H$ with
\[
 |V_1|=\cdots=|V_{q+1}|=q+1,
 \qquad \tau(H)=q+1.
\]
Every vertex belongs to an edge.

statements.name: cor:tree-cover
statements.text:
\label{cor:tree-cover}
For every sufficiently large prime $q$, there is a finite complete
graph with a $(q+1)$-edge-coloring whose vertices require exactly
$q+1$ monochromatic trees to cover. The same minimum holds for
connected monochromatic subgraphs.
